formation.title: The Formation of Punjab
formation.text:
The land of the five rivers stands united under a single banner. From the fertile Doabs watered by the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej to the ancient walls of Lahore, Punjab has always been a crossroads, of invaders and traders, of faiths and cultures, of East and West. Now, for the first time, a Punjabi state commands the loyalty of all these lands.

But what kind of Punjab shall this be? The martial traditions of the Khalsa call for a warrior state, where the sword and the scripture are wielded as one, and the Panth defends its sovereignty through strength of arms. Or shall Punjab embrace the legacy of its five rivers, a land of abundance and tolerance, where commerce flows as freely as the waters, and people of all faiths find shelter?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Khalsa Raj: the sovereignty of the Pure

modifiers.name: Khalsa Raj
modifiers.text: The Khalsa Raj proclaims sovereignty through the strength of the Panth. Every Sikh is a soldier, every soldier a saint, and the Punjab stands united under the double-edged sword of the Khanda.

options.text: The Five Rivers shall nourish all who dwell here

modifiers.name: Five Rivers Prosperity
modifiers.text: The land between the five rivers has always sustained great civilizations. With tolerance toward all faiths and mastery of irrigation and trade, Punjab flourishes as a crossroads of commerce and culture.

advances.name: Five Rivers Irrigation
advances.text: The Doab lands between the five rivers of Punjab yield extraordinary harvests when properly irrigated through canal systems and Persian wheels.

advances.name: Lahore's Schools of Learning
advances.text: Under the Ghaznavids and Delhi Sultanate, Lahore became a renowned center of Persian poetry, Islamic jurisprudence, and scholarly exchange.

advances.name: Doab Horsemen
advances.text: The flat plains between Punjab's rivers breed excellent cavalry, fast-moving horsemen accustomed to raiding and frontier warfare.

advances.name: Persian Wheel Technology
advances.text: The introduction of the Persian wheel transforms Punjab's agriculture, lifting water from deep wells to irrigate the dry uplands between the rivers, far from any bank.

advances.name: Crossroads of the Khyber
advances.text: Punjab guards the eastern terminus of the Khyber Pass, through which flow both conquerors and caravans. Control of this gateway means control of trade between Central Asia and India.

advances.name: Sultanate Garrison Tradition
advances.text: The cities of Punjab (Lahore, Multan, Sialkot) have served as fortress-cities on the Sultanate's northwestern frontier for centuries.

advances.name: Guru Nanak's Message
advances.text: In 1469, Guru Nanak was born in the Punjab village of Talwandi. His message ('There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim') proclaimed the unity of all humanity under one God, laying the foundation for Sikhism.

advances.name: Guru Ka Langar
advances.text: The community kitchen tradition established by the Sikh Gurus serves free meals to all visitors regardless of caste, creed, or station, a radical declaration of equality.

advances.name: Mughal Lahore
advances.text: Under the Mughals, Lahore becomes one of the great cities of the world. The Shalimar Gardens, the Badshahi Mosque, and the Lahore Fort transform the city into a jewel of Indo-Islamic civilization.

advances.name: Multan Indigo
advances.text: The southern Punjab around Multan develops extensive indigo plantations, producing the valuable blue dye for export across the subcontinent and beyond.

advances.name: Gurmukhi Script
advances.text: Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, standardizes the Gurmukhi script for recording Punjabi. This literary innovation ensures that the Sikh scriptures are accessible to common people, not locked in the Sanskrit of the elite.

advances.name: Gatka Tradition
advances.text: The Sikh martial art of gatka trains warriors in the use of the sword, shield, staff, and spear. It becomes central to the martial identity of the Khalsa.

advances.name: Guru Granth Sahib
advances.text: The compilation of the Adi Granth, later elevated to Guru Granth Sahib, brings together the hymns of Sikh Gurus, Hindu Bhakti saints, and Muslim Sufis in a scripture of unprecedented inclusivity.

event.title: The Eternal Guru
event.text:
The Adi Granth has been compiled, a sacred scripture unlike any other. It contains not only the hymns of the Sikh Gurus but the words of Hindu Bhakti saints and Muslim Sufi mystics, composed in multiple languages and musical modes. Guru Arjan has declared that the Granth shall reside in the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar, open to all who seek wisdom regardless of caste or creed.

In time, the tenth Guru will declare this scripture the eternal, living Guru of the Sikhs, a perpetual teacher that transcends any mortal authority. The Guru Granth Sahib embodies the revolutionary Sikh principle that divine truth belongs to no single people, language, or tradition, but speaks through all of them.

options.text: The Word is our Guru, now and forever

advances.name: Harmandir Sahib
advances.text: The foundation of the Golden Temple at Amritsar creates the spiritual heart of Sikhism, a temple built lower than its surroundings to teach humility, with doors open on all four sides to welcome all. It can be built at Sultanwind, the village on whose land Amritsar stands.

advances.name: Miri-Piri Doctrine
advances.text: Guru Hargobind wears two swords, Miri for temporal authority, Piri for spiritual authority. The doctrine establishes that Sikhs must be prepared to defend their faith by force of arms, and the Akal Sena, the first Sikh army, musters at Amritsar.

advances.name: Sikh Dharamsalas
advances.text: Networks of dharamsalas, rest houses and community centers, spread across Punjab, offering shelter and sustenance to travelers and pilgrims of all faiths.

advances.name: Akal Takht
advances.text: The Throne of the Timeless One, established at Amritsar by Guru Hargobind, becomes the supreme seat of Sikh temporal authority, the institution from which the Panth issues political and spiritual decrees.

advances.name: Five Rivers Trade
advances.text: The rivers of Punjab are arteries of commerce. Trade flows along their banks and through the Doab towns, connecting the markets of Central Asia with the wealth of the Gangetic plain.

advances.name: Khalsa Formation
advances.text: In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh institutes the Khalsa, the Order of the Pure. Through the ceremony of Khande ki Pahul, Sikhs are baptized as saint-soldiers, bound by a common identity that transcends caste.

event.title: The Baptism of the Double-Edged Sword
event.text:
On the day of Vaisakhi, before a gathering of thousands at Anandpur, the Guru called for volunteers willing to offer their heads for the faith. Five men stepped forward, a water-carrier, a farmer, a washerman, a barber, and a cook. No Kshatriya warriors, no Brahmin priests. The Guru baptized them with sweetened water stirred by a double-edged sword, and they became the Panj Pyare, the Five Beloved. Then, in an act that shattered every convention of caste and hierarchy, the Guru knelt and asked the Five to baptize him in turn.

The Khalsa was born, a fraternity where the lowest became the highest, where every member was both saint and soldier, where the surname Singh proclaimed that caste was abolished and every Sikh stood equal before the Almighty. This was not merely a military reform but a social revolution. How shall the Khalsa define itself?

options.text: We are forged in steel: the sword is our scripture

modifiers.name: Baptism of Steel
modifiers.text: The Khande ki Pahul has forged the Khalsa into warriors without peer. Every initiated Sikh carries steel and stands ready to defend the faith unto death.

options.text: We are the pure: our brotherhood is our strength

modifiers.name: Brotherhood of the Pure
modifiers.text: The Khalsa is more than an army. It is a brotherhood of equals bound by devotion, where caste holds no meaning and every member serves the community through selfless service.

advances.name: Misl Cavalry
advances.text: The twelve Misls of the Sikh Confederacy field fast-moving cavalry that excels at guerrilla warfare, raiding Mughal and Afghan supply lines across the Punjab plains.

advances.name: Dal Khalsa
advances.text: The Dal Khalsa unifies the Sikh military assembly. Though the Misls remain independent, they gather under the banner of the combined Khalsa for major campaigns.

advances.name: Khalsa Coinage
advances.text: The Sikh confederacy mints its own coins, the Nanakshahi rupee, bearing the names of the Gurus rather than any temporal sovereign, asserting Sikh monetary sovereignty.

advances.name: Rakhi System
advances.text: Sikh Misls levy the Rakhi, a protection tax on villages in exchange for defense against raiders and invaders. It becomes the fiscal foundation of Sikh territorial control.

advances.name: Akali Warriors
advances.text: The Akalis, 'Followers of the Timeless One', are the fearless vanguard of the Khalsa. Heavily armed with traditional weapons, they refuse European training and fight with the ferocity of religious devotion. Their companies can be raised as shock troops.

advances.name: Ranjit Singh's Empire
advances.text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh unites the twelve Misls under his personal rule, establishing the Sikh Empire with its capital at Lahore. His reign brings unprecedented stability, religious tolerance, and military power to Punjab. The chiefs who once led the Misls now ride for him as the Ghorcharas, the irregular horse of the court.

event.title: The Lion of the Punjab
event.text:
From a one-eyed boy who lost his father at age twelve, to the unquestioned master of the Punjab, the Maharaja's rise is the stuff of legend. He united the fractious Misls not through bloodshed alone, but through cunning diplomacy, strategic marriages, and the force of his personality. He captured Lahore at nineteen, without firing a shot.

Now the Maharaja turns his gaze to the army. He has recruited European officers, veterans of Napoleon's campaigns, to drill his infantry in the French manner and organize his artillery on modern principles. The Fauj-i-Khas, his model brigade, already rivals any force on the subcontinent. The ancient Zamzama cannon, captured from the Afghans, stands before the gates of Lahore as a symbol of Sikh power.

The question is whether this military revolution shall serve conquest or consolidation.

options.text: The Lion roars: let our enemies tremble

modifiers.name: Lion of Lahore
modifiers.text: The Maharaja has brought European discipline to the Khalsa army. With French-trained infantry, reformed artillery, and a united command, the Sikh Empire fields the finest native army on the subcontinent.

options.text: The Sarkar-i-Khalsa shall govern with wisdom

modifiers.name: Sarkar-i-Khalsa
modifiers.text: The government of the Khalsa brings stability and prosperity to Punjab. Under enlightened rule, the five rivers nourish a land of commerce, culture, and religious harmony.

advances.name: Fauj-i-Khas
advances.text: The Fauj-i-Khas is the elite model brigade of the Khalsa army, French-trained infantry, British-modeled cavalry, and a troop of artillery under European officers. It is the finest native force on the subcontinent.

advances.name: Lahore Foundry
advances.text: Under European supervision, Punjab develops modern artillery foundries at Lahore. The Khalsa cannon crews achieve extraordinary precision, rivaling any artillery in the world.

advances.name: Amritsar Shawl Trade
advances.text:
Amritsar becomes the hub of the Kashmiri shawl trade. Over a hundred thousand artisans weave, dye, and embroider fine shawls for export to Europe and the courts of Asia.

Available in: Shawl Karkhana

advances.name: Khalsa Modernization
advances.text: The Sikh Empire recruits European officers, veterans of the Napoleonic Wars, to modernize training, logistics, and tactics. Ranjit Singh transforms a feudal cavalry force into a modern combined-arms army.

advances.name: The Golden Temple
advances.text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh covers the upper floors of the Harmandir Sahib with 750 kilograms of pure gold, transforming the spiritual heart of Sikhism into one of the most magnificent religious structures in the world.

advances.name: Khalsa Regular Army
advances.text: The modern Khalsa army fields well-drilled regulars equipped with European muskets and bayonets, organized into battalions with professional non-commissioned officers.

advances.name: Punjabi Industry
advances.text: The workshops and forges of Lahore and Amritsar expand into proto-industrial production, manufacturing arms, textiles, and metalwork.

advances.name: Sikh Constitutional Governance
advances.text: The tradition of the Gurmata, collective decision-making by the Khalsa Panth at the Akal Takht, evolves into a sophisticated system of governance balancing military, religious, and civil authority.

advances.name: Punjab Breadbasket
advances.text: Punjab's fertile Doab lands and expanded canal irrigation make it the breadbasket of the subcontinent, feeding millions and generating agricultural surplus for export.

advances.name: Sikh Martial Legacy
advances.text: The martial traditions of the Khalsa endure across generations. The Sikh warrior ethos (courage, discipline, and readiness to sacrifice) becomes legendary across the world.

advances.name: Punjabi Renaissance
advances.text: A flowering of Punjabi literature, music, and artistic expression builds on the foundation of the Gurmukhi script and the cultural synthesis fostered by centuries of Sikh, Hindu, and Muslim coexistence.

destiny.name: Punjab's Destiny
destiny.text: Punjab stands united. The land of the five rivers has chosen its path, now it must be forged through action, conquest, and industry.

event.title: The Destiny of Punjab
event.text:
The five rivers flow eternal, but the state that commands them must prove itself worthy of permanence. Punjab stands at a crossroads, not merely of geography, where the passes of Central Asia meet the plains of Hindustan, but of destiny itself. The choices made now will determine whether this nation becomes a footnote in the chronicles of greater empires, or whether it carves its own name into the stone of history.

The path has been chosen. Now it must be walked.

destiny.name: Sword of the Panth
destiny.text: Secure the northern frontier by conquering Kashmir and building an army worthy of the Khalsa. Own Srinagar with at least 30,000 soldiers under arms.

conditions.text: Own Srinagar, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Sword Unsheathed
event.text:
The Vale of Kashmir has fallen to the armies of Punjab. Where once the Mughal governors and Afghan warlords contested this paradise of mountains and lakes, the banner of the Khalsa now flies over Srinagar. The northern frontier is secured, but this is only the beginning.

The mountains that once sheltered Punjab's enemies are now its rampart. From these heights, the warriors of the Panth look westward toward Kabul and southward toward Delhi. The sword of the Khalsa, once drawn, does not rest until its destiny is fulfilled.

options.text: The frontier is ours: now we look beyond it

destiny.name: March to Kabul
destiny.text: Carry the Khalsa banner into Afghanistan, conquering the ancient seat of Ghaznavid power. Hold Kabul with high prestige, and build Peshawar, the gate of the Khyber, into the fortress of the frontier.

conditions.text: Own Kābul, or a subject owns it
We hold Peshawar and it has at least 48 development

event.title: The Fall of Kabul
event.text:
The ancient city of Kabul (seat of the Ghaznavids who once plundered Punjab, stronghold of the Durrani who terrorized Lahore) has fallen to the Khalsa. The irony is not lost on the veterans of the campaign: the descendants of those who suffered the depredations of Afghan invaders have carried their standard to the very heart of Afghanistan.

The capture of Kabul transforms Punjab from a regional power into a subcontinental one. But with conquest comes the question of how to govern these new territories. Shall the army press forward with the momentum of victory, or shall discipline and order be imposed on the expanding frontier?

options.text: Press the advantage: the vanguard leads

modifiers.name: Khalsa Vanguard
modifiers.text: The Khalsa vanguard drives the advance, reinforcing quickly and plundering the wealth of conquered lands to fuel further campaigns.

options.text: Discipline above all: consolidate the frontier

modifiers.name: Frontier Discipline
modifiers.text: Iron discipline sustains the Khalsa on the Afghan frontier, reducing war weariness and attracting mercenaries to the banner, though the forts of the frontier are costly to keep.

destiny.name: Empire of the Khalsa
destiny.text: Build the greatest Sikh Empire the world has ever seen, stretching from Kandahar to Delhi. Own both cities with a massive treasury and army.

conditions.text: Own Kandahār, or a subject owns it
Own Delhi, or a subject owns it

event.title: Empire Without Peer
event.text:
From the passes of Kandahar to the walls of Delhi, from the snows of Kashmir to the deserts of Sindh, the Khalsa Empire now stretches across the breadth of the subcontinent's northwest. No power on earth has matched this achievement, an empire forged not from dynastic inheritance but from the collective will of the Panth.

The Zamzama cannon, 'the Fire-Breathing Dragon', stands before the gates of Lahore as a symbol of what the Khalsa has wrought. But every empire faces the choice between the sword that conquers and the hand that governs. Shall Punjab project its military power outward, demanding submission from its neighbors? Or shall the empire's intelligence and diplomacy bind its conquests into a lasting dominion?

options.text: The Lion roars: let them tremble

modifiers.name: Lion of Punjab
modifiers.text: The Lion of Punjab dictates terms to defeated foes, annexing territory at reduced cost and declaring wars with the confidence of the unconquered.

options.text: The thunder of Zamzama compels obedience

modifiers.name: Zamzama Thunder
modifiers.text: The thunder of Zamzama echoes across the empire, binding subjects through loyalty and intelligence networks; though the cost of empire strains the treasury.

destiny.name: Rivers of Gold
destiny.text: Transform Punjab's cotton wealth into commercial dominance. Accumulate gold and ensure cotton flows through the capital market.

children.text: Cotton is produced in the market
Cotton is traded in the market

event.title: The Rivers Yield Their Wealth
event.text:
The great cotton caravans of Punjab have begun to flow, from the fields of the Doab to the markets of the capital, from the spinning wheels of Multan to the trading houses of Lahore. Cotton is white gold, and Punjab sits atop an ocean of it.

The five rivers that give this land its name are more than waterways for irrigation and navigation. They are arteries of commerce, carrying the raw wealth of the interior to the markets of the world. The merchant who controls the confluence controls the trade of half a continent.

options.text: The rivers shall make us rich

destiny.name: Crossroads of Faith
destiny.text: Make Punjab a beacon of learning and tolerance by raising Amritsar, founded on the village land of Sultanwind, from a village into a town of pilgrims and merchants.

conditions.text: We hold Sultanwind (Amritsar) and it has grown into a town or become the seat of a market
We hold Sultanwind (Amritsar) and it has at least 50 development

event.title: Where All Faiths Meet
event.text:
Punjab has become what Guru Nanak envisioned, a land where Hindu and Muslim, Sikh and Christian, merchant and mystic find common ground. The growth of Amritsar from a village into a town has turned its bazaars, and those of Lahore, into centers of international finance. Money, like water, flows where the channels are deepest, and Punjab's channels run deep indeed.

The question now is how to leverage this prosperity. Shall the wealth of the Doab feed the growth of the land itself, turning Punjab into a garden of abundance? Or shall the community kitchen of the langar feed not just bodies but the integration of all peoples into a single Punjabi identity?

options.text: The Doab shall overflow with abundance

modifiers.name: Doab Abundance
modifiers.text: The fertile Doab lands yield such abundance that separatism fades and new diplomatic channels open, drawing neighbors into Punjab's orbit.

options.text: The langar feeds all who come

modifiers.name: Langar of Nations
modifiers.text: Punjab's legendary hospitality integrates diverse peoples and attracts mercenaries at low cost, though the comfort of prosperity dulls the army's edge on campaign.

destiny.name: Breadbasket of Nations
destiny.text: Become the commercial heart of the subcontinent. Cut Doab canals from the rivers in five places, secure the Sindh trade port of Thatta, and amass great wealth.

conditions.text: A Doab Canal stands in at least 5 of our locations
Own Thatta, or a subject owns it

event.title: Heart of the Subcontinent
event.text:
The merchants of Thatta bow before the trading houses of Punjab. The canals of the Doab carry water to fields that feed half the subcontinent. From the salt mines of Khewra to the cotton fields of Multan, from the shawl workshops of Amritsar to the river ports of the five Doabs, Punjab has become the indispensable crossroads of South Asian commerce.

This is not an empire of the sword but an empire of the ledger book and the grain measure, and it is no less powerful for that. The question that remains is whether Punjab shall project this commercial power outward through diplomacy and trade, or whether it shall perfect its internal economy to become a self-sustaining civilization.

options.text: Our merchants shall reach every court

modifiers.name: Five Rivers Emporium
modifiers.text: Punjab's diplomats and livestock merchants reach every court on the subcontinent, though the nation's commitment to tolerance makes religious wars politically costly.

options.text: Our looms and fields feed the world

modifiers.name: Cultural Synthesis
modifiers.text: The confluence of Sikh, Hindu, and Muslim traditions transforms Punjab's workshops into engines of production, with wool and salt exports sustaining far-reaching supply networks.

units.name: Doab Horsemen
units.text: Fast-riding cavalrymen from the plains between Punjab's rivers, skilled in raiding and frontier skirmishing.

units.name: Lahori Garrison
units.text: Disciplined garrison infantry drawn from the fortified cities of Punjab, trained in the defense of walls and citadels.

units.name: Nihang Warriors
units.text: Fearless Akali shock troops of the Khalsa, heavily armed with traditional weapons and driven by unwavering religious devotion.

units.name: Misl Cavalry
units.text: Fast guerrilla horsemen of the Sikh Confederacy, expert at flanking maneuvers and lightning raids.

units.name: Fauj-i-Khas
units.text: Elite infantry of the Khalsa army, trained by European officers in modern tactics and drilled to the highest standards.

units.name: Khalsa Artillery
units.text: Modernized cannon crews of the Sikh Empire, trained by French and Italian officers to achieve extraordinary precision.

units.name: Khalsa Regulars
units.text: Well-drilled modern infantry of the reformed Khalsa army, equipped with European muskets and organized into professional battalions.

units.name: Akal Sena
units.text: The Guru's own army, raised by Hargobind after he girded on the two swords. Volunteers who bring their own arms and ask no pay: a few hundred men who do not give ground.

units.name: Akali Companies
units.text: Blue-clad Akalis with sword, steel quoit and towering turban. They refuse drill, armor and retreat, and the regulars form up behind the gap they leave.

units.name: Ghorchara
units.text: The irregular horse of the Lahore court: gentlemen in mail and silk, each armed and mounted at his own cost. Superb riders and fighters one by one, and no man's idea of a drilled regiment.

buildings.name: Doab Canal
buildings.text: An irrigation canal drawing water from Punjab's rivers to nourish the fertile Doab lands between them.

where.text: The location's raw material is Wheat

buildings.name: Persian Wheel Well
buildings.text: A rahat: a masonry well with a chain of clay pots turned by a pair of oxen. It waters the uplands between the rivers, where no canal can be cut.

buildings.name: Darbar Sahib
buildings.text: The temple in the pool of Amritsar, built lower than the ground around it and open on all four sides. Pilgrims come from every corner of Punjab, and many of them stay.

buildings.name: Gurdwara
buildings.text: A Sikh temple with a community kitchen that serves free meals to all visitors, embodying the Sikh principles of equality and selfless service.

buildings.name: Lahore Arsenal
buildings.text: A military foundry and arsenal producing modern firearms and artillery for the Khalsa army.

buildings.name: Shawl Karkhana
buildings.text: A textile workshop where artisans weave, dye, and embroider fine shawls for the luxury export trade.

children.text: Dyes is produced in the market

buildings.name: Dharamsala
buildings.text: A Sikh rest house and community center offering shelter and sustenance to travelers and pilgrims of all backgrounds.

buildings.name: Khalsa Training Ground
buildings.text: A modern military academy where European-trained officers drill the Khalsa army in combined-arms tactics.

buildings.name: Rakhi Post
buildings.text: A Sikh protection station where the Rakhi levy is collected from villages in exchange for defense against raiders and bandits.

buildings.name: Khalsa Durbar
buildings.text: The sovereign court of the Khalsa Empire, where military commanders and civil administrators meet under the authority of the Panth to govern the vast Sikh dominion.

buildings.name: Doab Mandi
buildings.text: A grand marketplace at the river crossings where the goods of Central Asia, the Gangetic plain, and the Deccan converge in Punjab's commercial embrace.

list.name: Sarbat Khalsa
list.text: The biennial assembly of the entire Khalsa, summoned to Amritsar at Baisakhi and Diwali. Sitting at the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir Sahib, the misl chiefs, the granthis, and the Akali jathedars resolved disputes and issued gurmatas (decrees taken in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib) on war, treaty, and excommunication. It was the gurmata of 1733 that elected Kapur Singh leader of the Dal Khalsa; through such convocations the eighteenth-century Sikhs sustained political unity without a central state. Ranjit Singh quietly ceased convening the Sarbat Khalsa after 1805, recognizing that its authority was incompatible with his own.

list.name: Misl Confederacy
list.text: The twelve cavalry confederacies that divided the Punjab between c. 1716 and 1799: Sukerchakia, Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Ramgarhia, Phulkian, Singhpuria, Krora Singhia, Nakkai, Faizullapuria, Karor Singhia, Nishanwalia, and Dallewalia. Each misl was an aristocratic war-band whose sardars held territory under the rakhi system: protection rent paid by villages to the band whose horsemen patrolled their fields. The confederacy could field tens of thousands of cavalry against Ahmad Shah Abdali's invasions, but answered to no single sovereign; Ranjit Singh subdued the misls one by one between 1799 and 1809, dispossessing those who would not submit and folding the rest into his standing army.

list.name: Khalsa Panth
list.text: The order of the pure, founded by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur on Baisakhi 1699 with the initiation of the Panj Pyare and the institution of amrit pahul. The Khalsa fused religious devotion and military service: every initiated Sikh became a Singh or Kaur, bound by the five kakars and the Rahit Maryada code, and obligated to bear arms in defence of dharma. The Panth sustained Sikh resistance through the genocidal Mughal persecutions of the 1740s and 1750s, when Banda Singh Bahadur and the Dal Khalsa fought from the forests of Lakhi Jangal, and remained the moral foundation of every Sikh military formation thereafter.

list.name: Lahore Durbar
list.text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh's central court, established at Lahore on his coronation in 1801 and presided over by the vakil-i-mutlaq Dhian Singh Dogra. The Durbar issued firmans, audited provincial revenue, mediated between the sardars of the absorbed misls, and projected the maharaja's authority across a multi-religious Punjabi state stretching from Peshawar to the Sutlej. Through the Durbar Ranjit Singh assembled the Hindu Dogra brothers, the Punjabi Muslim Fakir Azizuddin, and a cadre of European advisers into a single administrative apparatus. The institution survived him only briefly: the regicidal struggles of 1839 to 1843 collapsed it within four years.

list.name: Fauj-i-Khas
list.text: The model brigade, raised by Ranjit Singh from 1822 and trained on French and Italian lines by veterans of Napoleon's armies. Jean-Francois Allard organized the cavalry, Jean-Baptiste Ventura the infantry, Claude-Auguste Court the artillery, and Paolo di Avitabile the gendarmerie of the Khyber frontier. The Khalsa Army's elite division drilled in three languages, fought in disciplined line and column, and fielded a horse artillery rivalled in Asia only by the East India Company's. Hari Singh Nalwa wielded the Fauj-i-Khas at the conquests of Multan, Kashmir, and Peshawar, breaking three centuries of Afghan ascendancy on the Indus before his death at Jamrud in 1837.

list.name: Daftar-i-Bahi
list.text: The revenue ledger system administered from Lahore by Diwan Sawan Mal of Multan and Diwan Dina Nath, who built on the late Mughal jagirdari but registered every grant in a permanent bahi (account-book). Sikh jagirs were attached to military service rather than hereditary right: a sardar who failed to deliver his contingent of horsemen forfeited the assignment back to the khalsa lands. The Daftar's scribes were drawn from Punjabi Khatri burghers and from the Brahmin Pandit class, and kept revenue rolls in Persian, Punjabi, and Landa scripts simultaneously, allowing the maharaja to tax a multi-confessional realm from a single treasury.

list.name: Akali Nihangs
list.text: The immortal warriors of the Akal Takht, the blue-clad ascetic order founded by Guru Hargobind in 1606 to embody the principle of miri-piri: temporal and spiritual sword in one. The Nihangs formed the orthodoxy guard of the Khalsa, served as guides on Sikh battlefields from Chamkaur (1704) to the Anglo-Sikh wars, and famously held Akali Phula Singh's jathedari against Ranjit Singh himself in the Lahore Durbar of 1819, when the Akali jathedar publicly fined the maharaja for moral lapses. In 1809 his Akalis fell upon the escort of the British envoy Metcalfe at Amritsar. The order answered to the Guru Granth Sahib and the rahit, not to a court, and its independence was a guarantor of Sikh orthodoxy against royal accommodation.
